nodes.name: Hydrothermal NiCr-LDH growth
nodes.procedure: The pristine NiCr-LDH nanosheets (denoted as NiCr-LDH) were first grown on the surface of nickel foam by a facile hydrothermal process.
nodes.source_text: The pristine NiCr-LDH nanosheets (denoted as NiCr-LDH) were first grown on the surface of nickel foam by a facile hydrothermal process.

nodes.name: Solvothermal acid etching
nodes.procedure: Then, the NiCr-LDH reacted with naphthalene-2,6-dicarboxylic acid (NDC) through a solvothermal method, and in situ transformed into ultrathin NiCr-LDH nanosheet arrays. In this procedure, deprotonated H+ from the NDC can partially etch the interlayer anions to form ultrathin nanosheets and metal hydroxide layers to create atomic vacancies.
nodes.source_text: Then, the NiCr-LDH reacted with naphthalene-2,6-dicarboxylic acid (NDC) through a solvothermal method, and in situ transformed into ultrathin NiCr-LDH nanosheet arrays.

nodes.characterization_summary: NiCr-LDH shows stacked nanosheets with lateral size 100-300 nm and thickness ~22.0 nm; NiCr-LDH NSAs shows vertically arranged ultrathin nanosheets with thickness 3.75 nm.
nodes.evidence_snippet: Scanning Electron Microscopy (SEM), transmission electron microscopy (TEM), and atomic force microscopy (AFM) images (Fig. 1b, S1a and S2†.) show that the pristine NiCr-LDH nanosheets with a lateral size of 100−300 nm and a thickness of ∼22.0 nm stack together disorderly.

properties.description: High magnification SEM showing porous structure

nodes.characterization_summary: NiCr-LDH NSAs shows ultrathin nanosheets with fringe lattice parameter 0.23 nm indexed to (015) planes of LDHs and atomic vacancies observed.
nodes.evidence_snippet: The high-resolution TEM (HRTEM, inset of Fig. 1e and S1b†) images show that the fringe lattice parameter of both samples were determined to be 0.23 nm indexed to the (015) planes of LDHs.

nodes.characterization_summary: NiCr-LDH NSAs single sheet thickness measured as 3.75 nm.
nodes.evidence_snippet: after further acid treatment, NiCr-LDH NSAs arranged vertically and were interconnected with each other on the Ni foam skeletons, and the thickness of a single sheet was only 3.75 nm (Fig. 1c–f).

nodes.characterization_summary: EDS mapping shows homogeneous distributions of Ni, Cr, and O elements in NiCr-LDH NSAs.
nodes.evidence_snippet: The EDS mapping images in Fig. 1g clearly indicate homogeneous distributions of Ni, Cr, and O elements in the NiCr-LDH NSAs.

nodes.characterization_summary: X-ray diffraction patterns show phase structure of NiCr-LDH NSAs did not change appreciably compared to NiCr-LDH.
nodes.evidence_snippet: The X-ray diffraction patterns in Fig. S3† show that the phase structure of NiCr-LDH NSAs did not change appreciably.

nodes.characterization_summary: NiCr-LDH NSAs shows Ni–O coordination number N=5.5 (vs 5.9 in NiCr-LDH) and Ni–M coordination number 5.4 (vs 5.6), indicating oxygen vacancies and metal vacancies with dangling bonds.
nodes.evidence_snippet: Quantitatively, we fitted the Ni K-edge k3-weighted EXAFS spectra of NiCr-LDH NSAs and NiCr LDH with the results in Fig. S4b, c and Table S1†. It can be seen that the Ni–O octahedral coordination number (N=5.5) of NiCr-LDH NSAs is lower than that in the NiCr-LDH (N=5.9)

nodes.characterization_summary: Similar coordination structure changes observed at Cr K-edge for NiCr-LDH NSAs compared to NiCr-LDH.
nodes.evidence_snippet: Similarly, according to Cr K-edge FT-EXAFS of NiCr-LDH NSAs and NiCr-LDH (Fig. 2b, S5b, c and Table S2†), similar conclusions can be drawn.

nodes.characterization_summary: NiCr-LDH NSAs Ni 2p peaks at 874.5 eV (2p1/2) and 856.8 eV (2p3/2), positive shifted 0.4 eV vs NiCr-LDH; Cr 2p peaks positive shifted 0.8 eV with Cr–OH at 579.7 eV and Cr–O at 578.0 eV.
nodes.evidence_snippet: In the high-resolution Ni 2p XPS spectra, the characteristic peaks at binding energies of 874.5 and 856.8 eV can be assigned to Ni 2p1/2 and 2p3/2 for NiCr-LDH NSAs, which are obviously positive-shifted by 0.4 eV compared with that of NiCr-LDH (874.1 and 856.4 eV, Fig. 2c).

nodes.characterization_summary: NiCr-LDH NSAs static contact angle 17° vs NiCr-LDH 33°, 50% reduction indicating significantly reduced interfacial tension and super-hydrophilic surface.
nodes.evidence_snippet: Fig. 4c shows an unexcepected static contact angle of 17° for NiCr-LDH NSAs, which corresponds to a significant reduction of 50% compared to NiCr-LDH.

nodes.characterization_summary: NiCr-LDH NSAs possesses Cdl of 36.3 mF cm^-2, larger than NiCr-LDH NS powders (34.2 mF cm^-2) and NiCr-LDH (27.9 mF cm^-2), indicating more exposed active sites.
nodes.evidence_snippet: The NiCr-LDH NSAs possess the largest Cdl of 36.3 mF cm^-2, compared to NiCr-LDH NS powders (34.2 mF cm^-2) and NiCr-LDH (27.9 mF cm^-2)

nodes.characterization_summary: Operando EIS shows NiCr-LDH NSAs has lower charge transfer resistance Rct than NiCr-LDH with increasing potential, indicating faster charge transfer.
nodes.evidence_snippet: the Rct of NiCr-LDH NSAs is obviously lower than that of NiCr-LDH with increasing potential, suggesting a faster charge transfer and more favorable reaction kinetics

nodes.characterization_summary: Operando SR-FTIR shows absorption band at 1075 cm^-1 assigned to *OOH species on NiO6-x sites, intensity increases with voltage; no band observed for NiCr-LDH.
nodes.evidence_snippet: a new absorption band located at around 1075 cm^-1 is observed in the operando SR-FTIR spectra of NiCr-LDH NSAs at an OER potential of 1.4 V, which can be assigned to the surface *OOH species.
